Milky Way - Beyond the Stars

We are Milky Way. A team of future space pioneers. We are united by a shared passion for science, technology, and the unknown. We believe that the boldest ideas can serve as the starting point for great discoveries

By participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to transform curiosity into innovation, knowledge into solutions, and teamwork into a force capable of shaping the future

Our mission is to think big, create boldly, and explore the new together
summary:
SPACE EXPLORERS is a story-driven space game for children aged 7–12. Kids follow one connected mission: they fly the ship “Aurora” and keep it working through hands-on mini-games, land on the Moon’s south pole, and then survive there day by day. Every morning Mission Control sends a forecast. During the day kids spend a limited budget on oxygen, power, heat and radiation shielding, and no choice is free. In the evening the forecast threat arrives, and a debrief explains what the child’s choices changed.

The game meets the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge with real NASA data. Solar flares come from NASA DONKI and are shown live when the API is reachable, or from a clearly labeled archive. Radiation doses are based on Curiosity RAD measurements, and Mission Control speaks with the real radio delay. Physics cards turn each episode into a lesson.

The game also builds the soft skills real crews need: if–then planning, a calm breathing pause, recognizing a crewmate’s emotions and teamwork. Up to four players can play on one Wi‑Fi network. Failure is always safe and explained, and the game has no accounts and no purchases. It runs in Russian and English, with Kazakh in progress.
details:
SPACE EXPLORERS: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

What does it do and how does it work?

SPACE EXPLORERS is a story-driven space game for children aged 7–12. It answers the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”. The player follows one connected mission in three acts:

The flight on the ship “Aurora”. The ship has 9 rooms and the crew flies for two in-game days. Children walk between consoles and complete 24 hands-on mini-games, such as connecting wires, balancing power, checking life support and caring for the ship’s pet. On a touch panel they steer the ship around asteroids. After each episode a short physics card explains one real idea behind what they just did. There are 9 cards, each in a Junior and an Advanced version.

Landing on the Moon near the south pole. The player controls thrust and tilt and has to answer the real “1202” alarm from Apollo 11. A live checklist turns each touchdown rule green or red: down speed, sideways speed, tilt and flat ground. If the landing is aborted, a “was / needed” table explains what went wrong. Then the child can try again, with an optional helper.

Surviving on the Moon. Each in-game day has three parts:

Morning: Mission Control sends a forecast, such as a cold snap, a dust cloud, meteorites, an energy crisis or a breakdown.

Day: the crew works and spends earned coins on base upgrades. Every upgrade has a trade-off, so no choice is free.

Evening: the forecast threat arrives, and a report shows how the choices played out.

Solar flares come from real NASA DONKI events. When the API is reachable they are shown as LIVE. Otherwise the game uses a clearly labeled archive, and archived data is never shown as live.

The game tracks base stats (oxygen, power, heat, pressure, hull strength, radiation dose) and astronaut stats (suit oxygen, food, fatigue, suit wear). Children can play alone, with a friend in split-screen, or with up to 4 players on the same Wi-Fi. Each player picks a crew role: pilot, engineer, researcher or life support.

What benefits does it have?

It teaches through doing. Children make trade-offs between oxygen, power, shielding and science with a limited budget, the same way real mission planners do.

It builds calm habits, based on psychology research. Each briefing has an if–then plan (“If there is a flare, I go into the shelter”). A breathing pause is voluntary and never scored. Children practise naming a crewmate’s emotions and supporting them. Feedback describes actions, not the child’s personality.

Mistakes are safe. No crew member ever dies. After a failure the crew evacuates and the debrief explains why. Reflection questions have no wrong answers.

Kids stay busy and come back. The story, mini-games, achievements in 6 areas and cosmetic rewards keep them playing.

It is safe for children. There is no real money, no accounts and no free-text chat, only ready-made phrases and smileys. Players pick a callsign instead of typing their name. Progress is saved only in a local file.

What is the intended impact?

We want children to understand why space missions are hard: radiation, life support, communication delay, power limits and landing physics. We also want them to practise the teamwork and emotional skills real crews need. The game is designed for classrooms and families. It offers two age levels (Junior and Advanced) and three languages (Russian, Kazakh and English), so it can reach children in Kazakhstan who rarely get space education in their own language. A child should finish a session knowing real numbers and real reasons, not just that they “won”.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

Language and engine: Rust with the Bevy 0.16 game engine, as a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux.

Structure: the game rules live in a separate crate with no graphics code (ja-core), so they can be tested on their own. Graphics and sound are in a second crate.

Networking: our own UDP local-network multiplayer. The host computes all the rules, so the players’ computers never drift apart.

NASA data:

DONKI space weather API (flares, CMEs, geomagnetic storms, SEP events)

Curiosity RAD and Chang’e-4 LND radiation measurements

NASA Veggie / OSDR plant growth data

MOXIE oxygen production on Mars

NASA space communication delays

NASA-STD-3001 dose limits

Apollo 11 landing history

Content: missions, dialogs, ship rooms and physics cards live in JSON files. Teachers can edit them without touching code.

Testing: Monte Carlo balance tests play hundreds of simulated missions with a “careful” kid and a “careless” kid, to make sure every map can be won. An automated screenshot tour captures the game for documentation.

Hardware: ordinary laptops. The game supports keyboard, mouse, gamepads and touch screens (virtual joystick).

Assets: OpenMoji icons (CC BY-SA 4.0), Russo One and PT Sans fonts (OFL), and generated sound effects.

How is the project creative?

The whole game is one story (flight, landing, survival), not a set of separate quizzes. Each act uses what the child learned in the one before.

Real solar flares from NASA drive the game. The danger a child faces may match what the Sun actually did.

Mission Control messages arrive after the real radio delay. The “1202” alarm is a real moment from history that children experience themselves.

The landing debrief teaches through the mistake itself: it shows what each value was and what it needed to be, instead of just “Game Over”.

Emotional training is part of the gameplay. Supporting an upset crewmate is a mission task, not a separate lesson.

Crew roles give bonuses but forbid nothing, so teamwork happens naturally.

What factors did the team consider?

Age-appropriate design: big icon-first buttons, two difficulty levels, and forecasts that are accurate for younger kids but can be wrong for older ones, just like real forecasts.

Scientific honesty: game numbers are scaled so children can follow them, but the ratios and cause and effect come from real data. Game conventions are labeled as such, including the fictional ship “Aurora”, asteroids near the Moon and a lunar “dust storm”. Every source is listed on an in-game page.

Child safety and privacy: no personal data, no purchases, no open chat and no public rankings.

Accessibility: works offline with the archived data, runs on ordinary computers, supports several input methods and three languages.

Psychological wellbeing: no punishment for wrong answers, hints are free, and failure is a safe, explained step. The game does not assess real readiness for spaceflight and is not therapy.

Fair difficulty: checked with balance tests. These tests showed that Europa could not be won even by a careful player, so we moved its base under the ice.

Teamwork in development: the code was split into two parts so two developers could work in parallel. Teachers can manage content without programming.

NASA Open APIs (api.nasa.gov), used to access DONKI
Curiosity RAD radiation measurements (Mars surface and cruise dose)
NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), plant growth in space
NASA Veggie (growing plants on the ISS)
Mars 2020 Perseverance / MOXIE (oxygen from Mars air
NASA Space Communications: 7 Things You Need to Know (Earth–Moon–Mars delay)
NASA Human Research Program: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
